prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, I say pow. I slice my throat with a single stroke, pull an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we did together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air then thrusting our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call, blood only we saw. As well as death, we’d mime marriage. I’d slide on a spectral ring and you’d shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second till the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient at beginnings, the Air Year: the anniversary prior to paper for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust under my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, pow on the train, I suspend my non-knife above my head, “see what you’re making me do.” Red whirls rise from the cuts. All these huge thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Remember, Twiddling, Air

outputs.L1:
I press two fingers to my temple, cock my thumb, and say, “Pow.” I draw a single stroke across my throat, dragging an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Do you remember the deaths we performed together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air, then thrusting our chins forward to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play, when you slowly leaned forward to nick your femoral artery, then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call—the blood visible only to us.

Alongside death, we mimed marriage. I would slide on a spectral ring, and you would shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second, until the thought dissolved back into your skin. I am adept at beginnings: the Air Year, the anniversary before paper, for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear.

Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood covers the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust beneath my nails. I slit my throat at the traffic lights; I say “pow” on the train. I suspend my non-knife above my head: “See what you’re making me do.” Red whorls rise from the cuts. All these vast thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.
outputs.L2:
I press two fingers against my temple, cock my thumb, and say, “Bang.” I draw one clean line across my neck, dragging a make-believe knife upright along the vein. Do you remember all the ways we used to die together? How we would fiddle with imaginary oven dials, then jut our chins forward as if breathing in the gas? I adored you in that experimental performance, when you bent forward little by little to cut your femoral artery, then sat there bleeding silently until the curtain fell—blood visible only to us.

Alongside death, we acted out marriage too. I would slip a phantom ring onto your finger, and you would tremble at the charge of my thumb and forefinger closing the promise for an instant, before the idea dissolved back into your skin. I am good at first stages, at the Air Year: the anniversary before paper, the one marked by things that vanish. It was only once our rings turned into real silver that they disappeared for good.

Now the house has become a pantomime. Pretend blood is everywhere: across the floor, ground into the carpet threads, the shirts, the bras, dried into a weightless crust beneath my fingernails. At traffic lights, I cut my throat. On the train, I go pow. I hold my nonexistent knife above my head and say, “Look what you’re making me do.” Red spirals lift from the wounds. Every enormous thought ends in nothing. My shadow is the chalk mark around a woman who never leapt.
outputs.L3:
The speaker repeatedly stages acts of self-destruction through mime and imaginary gesture, using the body to express emotional pain without necessarily carrying those actions into reality. These gestures become a form of performance: a way of making inner suffering visible while keeping it at a symbolic distance. The speaker appears caught between the urge to dramatize grief and the inability, or refusal, to transform that drama into actual self-harm.

This pattern is connected to the memory of a past relationship. The speaker recalls a bond shaped by shared performances of death, intimacy, and imagined marriage. The relationship seems to have depended on theatrical gestures and fantasies, as though love itself was experienced through enactment rather than through stable reality. Death and marriage are imagined together, suggesting that intimacy was intertwined with danger, loss, and dramatic self-display.

The text also contrasts different stages of the relationship. In its early phase, the bond appears fragile, fleeting, and almost unreal, marked by gestures and performances that could disappear as quickly as they appeared. Later, this ephemeral connection is set against the solidity of silver rings, symbols of commitment and permanence. Yet paradoxically, once the relationship takes on this more fixed form, it seems to vanish. The rings remain as concrete objects, but the emotional bond they were meant to secure has disappeared or become unreachable.

The speaker’s home and everyday life are similarly haunted by what cannot be fully seen or resolved. Invisible traces of violence, grief, and emotional disturbance seem to linger in domestic space. Ordinary surroundings are charged with memory, as if past pain has left marks that cannot be physically located but are nevertheless deeply felt. The speaker inhabits a world where absence is as powerful as presence, and where unresolved feeling continues to shape perception.

Overall, the text suggests that the speaker’s thoughts of self-destruction belong primarily to the realm of imagination and performance. The gestures of self-harm are vivid and repeated, but they remain mimed rather than enacted. This distinction is important: the speaker’s dramatic impulses reveal intense suffering, but they also show that the violence is being expressed symbolically. The text therefore explores emotional pain through theatricality, memory, and haunting, presenting self-destruction less as an action than as an imagined language for grief.
outputs.L4:
The text explores the aftermath of a relationship’s collapse as a state of grief, lost intimacy, and self-destructive thought. Rather than presenting heartbreak in ordinary realistic terms, it turns emotional devastation into a series of surreal, theatrical images. Death, marriage, and violence appear not as straightforward events, but as symbolic performances: the body becomes a stage on which invisible pain is acted out. The use of mime-like imagery is especially important because it suggests suffering that cannot be fully spoken or seen, yet is still intensely present. Gestures, imagined wounds, and silent confrontations replace direct explanation, giving the emotional world of the speaker a strange but powerful physical form.

At the center of the text is the experience of absence. The lost lover is no longer fully present, but their disappearance continues to shape the speaker’s inner life. This absence becomes almost tangible, as if it can strike, cut, or haunt the body. The text suggests that intimacy does not simply vanish when a relationship ends; instead, it can remain as a painful imprint. Memories of closeness become inseparable from images of injury, and love is transformed into something ghostly, violent, and difficult to escape.

The references to marriage and death deepen this tension. Marriage usually symbolizes union, permanence, and shared life, while death represents final separation. By bringing these ideas together, the text shows how love can feel both sacred and destructive, both binding and annihilating. The collapse of the relationship becomes a kind of symbolic death, not only of the partnership but also of the self the speaker once inhabited within it. This is why the grief feels so extreme: the speaker is not merely mourning another person, but also mourning a vanished version of their own life.

The key result is a portrait of pain that feels both theatrically imagined and emotionally real. The surreal imagery does not distance the reader from the speaker’s suffering; instead, it makes that suffering more vivid. By presenting emotional wounds as if they were physical ones, the text reveals how deeply absence can hurt. It suggests that what is invisible is not necessarily less powerful, and that the end of intimacy can leave marks as vivid and lasting as any visible injury.
outputs.L5:
Remember the old ceiling fan in the corner of the room, twiddling slowly above us as if it had all the time in the world? Its blades sliced the warm air into lazy circles, carrying the scent of rain, dust, and distant summers.

I used to sit beneath it and think that air had memories. It moved through open windows, brushed past bookshelves, slipped under doors, and somehow kept the shape of every voice it had ever touched. If you listened closely enough, you could almost hear yesterday speaking.

So I remember: the quiet evenings, the soft hum, the restless fingers twiddling a pencil while thoughts drifted upward. Nothing important seemed to happen then, and yet those small moments stayed—floating, invisible, like air.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary flash fiction in first person about a breakup or failed marriage, using mime and imaginary violence as central metaphors. Make it surreal, poetic, darkly funny, and emotionally devastating.
counterfactuals.output:
On our last morning, my husband shot me with his finger.

He had always been an excellent mime of violence. At parties he could pull a grenade from his pocket, bite out the pin, and toss it into a bowl of olives; everyone would scream delightedly when the room exploded in silence. He could saw his own neck with an invisible knife, could hang himself from a ceiling hook that wasn’t there, could machine-gun the cat until she yawned and left.

But that morning, in the kitchen, he aimed at me over the cooling toast and said, “Bang.”

I looked down at my chest. A red flower had not appeared. Instead, the same old absence opened, neat and round. I pressed my palm over it.

“You missed,” I said.

“I never miss,” he said, and blew smoke from his fingertip.

Our marriage had been like this for years: a series of expertly performed murders in which nobody died enough to leave. He would strangle me with a rope made of air. I would stagger beautifully, tongue out, eyes bulging, then applaud him because the technique was good. I would push him down a flight of stairs we did not own. He would tumble in place through the living room, breaking imaginary bones, cursing the imaginary architect. Then we would eat soup.

Once, during a fight about the mortgage, I trapped him in a glass box. He flattened his palms against its invisible walls, his face distorted by my perfect nothing. I stood outside, arms crossed, pretending not to hear him. For three days he lived in there. I passed him coffee through a panel that opened only when I wanted to be kind. On the fourth day he stepped out and kissed me with the mouth of a man who had learned the dimensions of his prison and found them familiar.

We were funny, people said. Such chemistry. Such commitment to the bit.

No one noticed that after every dinner party, I swept up handfuls of invisible shrapnel. No one noticed the blood that wasn’t on the curtains. No one noticed how carefully we stepped around the bodies of the people we had been.

That morning, after he shot me, I walked to the hallway and took my coat from a hook shaped like a question mark. He followed, reloading his finger.

“Where are you going?” he asked.

I turned and drew an invisible bow. I pulled the string back until my elbow trembled, until the arrow hummed between us with everything I had not said: the baby we never had, the apology he stored in his throat like a swallowed coin, the way loneliness had learned to sleep between us and steal the blankets.

“Don’t,” he said, smiling, because he still thought pain required props.

I let go.

The arrow flew silently into him. He looked surprised. Then insulted. Then, at last, hurt.

He dropped to his knees in the foyer, clutching the place where his heart should have been more convincingly located. I wanted to laugh. I did laugh. It came out like a window breaking in another room.

“You’re being dramatic,” he whispered.

“Yes,” I said. “Finally.”

I opened the door. Outside, the street was full of white-faced mimes dragging invisible suitcases, leaving lovers trapped in invisible rooms, walking against winds that were not there and still somehow ruined their hair.

Behind me, my husband performed an immaculate death. He thrashed, gasped, reached toward me with one trembling hand. It was the best work of his life.

I almost stayed to watch the curtain fall.

Instead, I stepped through the doorway and felt, for the first time in years, the bullet arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem about a woman grieving a relationship through invisible gestures: pretend suicide, pretend weddings, phantom blood, and the idea of an “Air Year” anniversary before paper.
counterfactuals.output:
Before paper, there is air.

She calls it the Air Year, the first anniversary of what never learned to become official: no registry ink, no folded vows saved in a drawer, no photograph with everyone smiling toward the future as if it were a window. Only breath. Only the invisible architecture of two people once promising each other rooms inside themselves.

All year she rehearses ceremonies no one can attend. In the kitchen, she lifts an empty glass and marries him again to the hum of the refrigerator. In the hallway, she pins a veil of light to her hair and walks toward a door that does not open. At night she lies down beside the outline he left in the mattress and performs her small pretend deaths—not to end herself, but to show the ceiling how love can stop moving and still occupy a body.

Her hands become expert in absence. They button a shirt he is not wearing. They wipe phantom blood from the corner of a mouth that never apologizes. They set a second plate, then clear it before anything can grow cold. They sign his name in steam on the bathroom mirror and watch it vanish as if the house itself has decided to forget.

Some mornings she wakes with rice in her hair, though there has been no wedding. Some evenings her palms are red, though there has been no wound. Grief, she learns, is a theater of invisible gestures: the bouquet thrown to no one, the ring slipped onto air, the ambulance that never comes because the body is still breathing, stubbornly, inside its ruin.

On the Air Year, she opens every window.

Nothing enters dramatically. No messenger, no rain, no absolution. Just wind moving through the rooms with the intimacy of someone who once knew where everything was kept. It lifts the curtains. It touches her face. It turns the blank pages on the table, though she has not yet written a word.

Before paper, there is air.

And for the first time she understands: air is not nothing. Air is where the vow went when it could not live anywhere else. Air is the dress, the blood, the goodbye, the almost. Air is the anniversary she survives by breathing through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental monologue in the style of contemporary literary fiction, where the narrator describes a past love through mimed deaths and marriages, ending with an image of survival rather than actual death.
counterfactuals.output:
I practiced losing you before I knew I was practicing.

In the kitchen, for instance, with the blue bowl between us and the spoons shining like small, obedient witnesses, I would let my head fall back against the refrigerator and say, in a voice borrowed from a silent film actress, *I am dead now, please proceed accordingly.* You would place two fingers at my throat, solemn as a village doctor, and announce that the pulse had gone somewhere inland. Then you would cover my face with a dish towel. Then uncover it. Then kiss me back into the republic of breakfast.

We were always rehearsing catastrophe in domestic light.

On the bus, I died of a glance you gave a stranger. In bed, you died of my refusal to answer a question honestly. In the grocery store, between tomatoes and batteries, we took turns collapsing against the oranges, our bodies careful not to bruise anything we couldn’t afford to buy. We were young enough to think performance could protect us. Young enough to think that if we named the ending often and extravagantly, the ending itself would grow bored and wander off.

Once, at a party, we married seven times.

The first marriage took place beside the coat pile. You wore a scarf like a stole, and I held a plastic cup of warm wine as though it were an ancestral candle. A man we barely knew pronounced us “probably doomed,” which felt official enough. We kissed while someone’s cigarette burned a small dark mouth into the arm of the couch.

The second marriage happened in the bathroom, because I had been crying and you had been laughing and neither of us understood the difference. You drew a ring around my finger with eyeliner. I drew one around yours with toothpaste. We stood under the buzzing bulb, mint and black blooming on our hands, and promised what people promise when they don’t believe language is binding: always, never, only, mine.

By the fifth marriage, we had become strangers at a train station. By the sixth, we were widowed in advance. By the seventh, no one attended but the dog, who sneezed during the vows and was therefore the most honest among us.

Later, walking home, we staged our joint funeral in the snow.

You lay down first, arms folded with irritating elegance. I complained that you were making death look like a magazine advertisement. You said I was jealous because even my grief had bad posture. Then I lay down beside you, and the cold entered my coat with the seriousness of a letter from the government. Above us, the sky was a flat gray sheet someone had forgotten to change. Our breath rose and vanished, rose and vanished, like souls in a child’s drawing.

“Do you think anyone will remember us?” you asked.

“Not accurately,” I said.

You laughed, and the snow took the shape of your laughter for one second before it became weather again.

This is the part I return to: not the end, not even one of the endings we invented, but the small labor of getting up. Your hand searching for mine without ceremony. My knees wet. Your hair full of white. The two of us staggering upright, resurrected badly, brushing each other off with all the tenderness of people who had not yet learned that tenderness is sometimes just delay.

We did not last, which is not the same as dying.

There were years after you. This remains astonishing. There were apartments where your name was never said aloud. There were mornings that opened without your face in them and did not immediately close. I bought pears and let them ripen. I answered emails. I became, in small public ways, reliable. When friends asked about you, I performed a reasonable version of myself. I did not clutch my chest. I did not fall elegantly beside the bread. I did not request a towel for my face.

Still, the body keeps its theater.

A certain song enters a café and I am widowed by the sugar packets. A woman on a bicycle wears your green coat and I marry the traffic light, the curb, the hour before rain. In hotel rooms, I sometimes wake as one half of an old ritual: bride, corpse, witness, fool. My hands find no eyeliner, no toothpaste ring. Only the sheet, twisted and ordinary, clinging to my legs like surf.

I have tried to tell the story cleanly. We loved. We failed. We left. But the truth is more ceremonial and less useful. We were always dressing the wound before the wound arrived. We walked toward separation wearing veils. We built little coffins out of jokes. We mistook rehearsal for immunity, drama for prophecy, intimacy for the right to be cruel and forgiven in the same breath.

And yet—

here I am, speaking.

Not from beyond anything. Not as a ghost tapping at the glass. Not as the tragic woman under the dish towel, waiting for your mouth to restore me. I am not restored. I am not ruined. I am a person standing at the sink after midnight, rinsing one cup, then another. Outside, the trees keep their difficult balance. A moth worries the window and does not understand the window. My own reflection hovers there, pale, unburied, still making faces at the dark.

I lift my hand.

The reflection lifts its hand.

We go on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a dark, uncanny flash fiction piece about two lovers who used to act out imaginary deaths together, and now after separation the narrator keeps performing them in public. Use vivid bodily imagery but make everything metaphorical/invisible.
counterfactuals.output:
We used to rehearse our deaths the way other couples rehearsed weddings.

In the kitchen you would lean back against the sink, one hand at your throat, and say, *Oh no, the moon has lodged itself in my windpipe.* I would rush to you with both hands full of imaginary silver, pretending to pry the light from your mouth. You would make a sound like a cello being buried. Then you would slide down the cabinet, laughing so hard your knees knocked the pans awake.

In bed I died of roses. In the bath you drowned in birds. On the living room rug we took turns being stabbed by weather, poisoned by hymns, strangled by the long black ribbon of Sunday evening. Nothing ever touched us. There were no knives, no bruises, no blood—only the theater of it, the way your face emptied so beautifully when you pretended to leave it. You had a gift for absence. Even then.

After you left, I found I could not stop.

At the post office, between the envelopes and the woman buying stamps with flowers on them, I felt the old cue arrive: a soft pressure behind the ribs, a hand made of fog closing over the heart. I staggered against the counter. The clerk asked if I was all right. I wanted to tell him I had been struck by a cathedral falling from a great height, that my organs were now full of bells. Instead I nodded, paid for postage, and collapsed inwardly with great precision.

No one saw.

That became the problem, and the seduction.

I began dying everywhere.

On buses I let invisible eels coil through my lungs. In grocery aisles I was devoured by fruit, my belly split sweetly by unseen pomegranates, my tongue blackened by phantom plums. In the laundromat, while socks revolved in their little weather systems, I suffered an immaculate electrocution. My bones lit up like a saint’s behind stained glass. A child dropped his juice box and stared, but only because I had smiled too widely.

I learned to keep my body ordinary. That was the art. Shoulders level. Hands unclenched. Breath passing in and out like an obedient animal. Meanwhile, beneath the skin, entire operas of ruin unfolded. My liver became a moth-wing. My spine filled with snow. My heart unstitched itself, thread by red thread, though nothing reddened, nothing spilled. I died so quietly that strangers stood close enough to touch me and never knew they were warm beside a corpse.

Sometimes I imagined you watching.

You would have criticized my technique. *Too much jaw,* you’d say. *Too much hunger in the eyes. Death is not a plea. It’s a door left open.*

You were always better at endings.

I saw you once after the separation, or thought I did, outside the museum where they keep the saints behind glass. You were across the street in a dark coat, your face turned away, your hair lifted by the wind like smoke deciding against a chimney. At once I began one of our old favorites: the one where a swarm of invisible bees builds a hive in the chest. I stood very still as they filled me. Wax in the ventricles. Honey in the throat. The queen settling behind the sternum with her terrible crown.

When the light changed, you crossed with the others.

You passed within arm’s length.

I died magnificently.

My knees did not buckle. My mouth did not open. Not one bee escaped. But inside me the hive split, golden and catastrophic, and every chamber of my body flooded with sweetness so dense it became indistinguishable from grief.

You did not turn.

After that, my performances grew more elaborate. I died of mirrors in department stores. I died of wolves in the financial district. I died of a piano lowered by angels through the ceiling of a pharmacy. I perfected the look of a man carrying his own invisible autopsy beneath his coat.

People began to notice something, though not what.

Women moved their handbags away from me. Men glanced up from their phones, frowning, as if they’d smelled rain underground. Dogs whined. Automatic doors opened too early when I approached, then closed too late behind me. Once, in a crowded train, every passenger fell silent at the exact moment I began to asphyxiate on a bouquet of unseen lilies. For three stops, no one spoke. Even the train seemed to hold its breath.

I wondered if death, even make-believe, leaves a residue.

Perhaps I was staining the air.

Perhaps each performance shed some transparent organ, some ghostly intestine or lung, and the city was filling with my discarded interiors. Commuters stepped through them daily: veils of heart, ribbons of bowel, the pale parachutes of lungs opening above intersections. Lovers kissed inside the steam of my vanished marrow. Pigeons strutted through the invisible meat of me.

And you—where were you? Were you still alive in the plain, administrative sense? Did you eat toast, answer emails, sleep on your left side? Or had you gone on dying too, privately, beautifully, in rooms I would never enter?

Last night, in the lobby of a hotel where I had no reason to be, I performed our first death.

The simplest one.

You invented it on a Tuesday, years ago, while rain scratched softly at the windows. One lover stands across from the other and says nothing. The silence sharpens. The silence enters. There is no wound, but the body understands it has been opened.

In the hotel lobby, beneath a chandelier trembling with false stars, I stood among travelers dragging wheeled suitcases over the marble. Their faces shone with the exhaustion of having destinations. I let the silence find me.

It entered cleanly.

Not through the mouth or the chest, but through the place your name had occupied. The old aperture. The private fontanelle. I felt it pass into me, long and cold, dividing thought from thought. Around me, people checked in, checked out, asked for extra towels, complained about the minibar. Inside, I bloomed open like a dark flower no one had planted.

Then someone behind me whispered my name.

Not loudly. Not even with certainty.

But my body knew your voice before my mind could defend itself. Every invisible death I had ever rehearsed rose at once inside me, a parliament of catastrophes. Moon in the throat. Birds in the bathwater. Weather in the ribs. Bees in the heart. Roses, wolves, bells, snow.

I turned.

No one was there.

Only the revolving door, slowly turning, though no one entered and no one left. Only the night outside, pressing its face to the glass. Only my reflection layered over the street, pale and attentive, wearing an expression I recognized from your best performances.

The one that meant: *I have already gone.*

The one that meant: *Now you try.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, fragmented paragraph about heartbreak, performance, and absence. Include invisible weapons, spectral rings, a house like a mime scene, and the line or idea that “my shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.”
counterfactuals.output: The applause kept falling after you left, soft as dust, cruel as confetti, and I stood there smiling with invisible weapons tucked beneath my ribs, bowing to an audience of empty chairs. The house became a mime scene: doors I could not open, windows I could not lean through, a table set for gestures, a bed made of held breath. Around my fingers, spectral rings tightened and loosened, promises rehearsing their own vanishing act. I learned to perform absence beautifully — to enter a room as if I were still expected, to laugh where the script said laugh, to press my hand against the wall and pretend it pressed back. Outside, the night leaned over the balcony, patient, black-gloved, but my shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump. It stayed there, flat and faithful, proving nothing except that leaving can look like survival, and survival can look, from far away, like a final trick with no body, no blood, no curtain, only the silence clapping and clapping in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
